result:
I'd make curiosity and truth-seeking the default human impulse—stronger than tribal loyalty, comfort, or short-term status.

Most large-scale problems (avoidable disease, persistent poverty, conflict, stalled science, poor governance) aren't mainly limited by raw resources or intelligence. They're limited by motivated reasoning, inherited dogmas, and incentives that reward signaling over accuracy. A widespread, stubborn drive to understand how things actually work—and to update when evidence contradicts preferences—would compound. It would improve education, research, institutions, and cooperation without needing to dictate specific outcomes.

It's not a magic fix for human nature, and it wouldn't eliminate trade-offs or tragedy. But it removes one of the biggest self-imposed bottlenecks on progress. Everything else (health, energy, exploration, reduced suffering) gets easier once more people reliably prefer reality to narrative.

message.reasoning:
The question is: "If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?"
If I could change the world in one way, I'd make curiosity the default setting for every human mind. Not just a nice-to-have trait, but the default operating system—something so baked into how we think, learn, and interact that no one has to try to be curious anymore. 

Right now, too much of our energy goes to tribal loyalty, short-term comfort, and fear of the unknown. Curiosity flips that script: it turns strangers into collaborators, ideology into testable ideas, and suffering into solvable puzzles. It’s the single lever that could unwind poverty, disease, conflict, and the existential risks we’re already staring down.
